Background Gut damage allows translocation of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and fungal β-D-glucan (BDG) into the blood. This microbial translocation contributes to systemic inflammation and risk of non-AIDS comorbidities in people living with HIV, including those receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). We assessed whether markers of gut damage and microbial translocation were associated with cognition in ART-treated PLWH. Methods Eighty ART-treated men living with HIV from the Positive Brain Health Now Canadian cohort were included. Brief cognitive ability measure (B-CAM) and 20-item patient deficit questionnaire (PDQ) were administered to all participants. Three groups were selected based on their B-CAM levels. We excluded participants who received proton pump inhibitors or antiacids in the past 3 months. Cannabis users were also excluded. Plasma levels of intestinal fatty acid binding protein (I-FABP), regenerating islet-derived protein 3 α (REG3α), and lipopolysaccharides (LPS = were quantified by ELISA, while 1–3-β-D-glucan BDG) levels were assessed using the Fungitell assay. Univariable, multivariable, and splines analyses were performed. Results Plasma levels of I-FABP, REG3α, LPS and BDG were not different between groups of low, intermediate and high B-CAM levels. However, LPS and REG3α levels were higher in participants with PDQ higher than the median. Multivariable analyses showed that LPS association with PDQ, but not B-CAM, was independent of age and level of education. I-FABP, REG3α, and BDG levels were not associated with B-CAM nor PDQ levels in multivariable analyses. Conclusion In this well characterized cohort of ART-treated men living with HIV, bacterial but not fungal translocation was associated with presence of cognitive difficulties. These results need replication in larger samples. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12981-023-00525-z. Keywords People living with HIV Cognition Gut Microbial translocation LPS http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/501100000024 Canadian Institutes of Health Research MOP 103230 CIHR Team grant TCO 125272 http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/501100002879 Canadian HIV Trials Network, Canadian Institutes of Health Research CTN 273 FRQ-S Réseau SIDA/Maladies infectieuses issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2023 Background The gut mucosa plays key roles in physiology and health. By targeting mucosal CD4 T-cells, HIV profoundly affects gut homeostasis, promotes epithelial cell death and decreases cell–cell adhesion. Circulating markers of gut integrity have been used to characterized levels of leaky gut in people living with HIV (PLWH). Intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP) is released in the circulation upon gut epithelium cell death. I-FABP blood levels have been found elevated in PLWH taking or not antiretroviral therapy (ART) compared to control without HIV in numerous studies. Higher levels of regenerating islet-derived protein 3 α have also been found in PLWH, regardless of their use of ART, compared to controls [ 1 ]. REG3α is an antimicrobial peptide produced in the gut lumen. Upon gut damage, REG3α translocate in the submucosa and its presence in the circulation reflects gut permeability. HIV-associated gut damage allows passage of microbial products in the submucosa and systemic circulation. This microbial translocation is commonly characterized by quantification of bacterial product lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in blood. Indeed, LPS levels have been shown elevated in both ART-naïve and ART-treated PLWH. Translocation of fungal products β-D-glucan (BDG) has also been described during HIV infection and elevated blood levels of BDG persist in ART-treated PLWH [ 2 , 3 ]. Both bacterial and fungal products have been shown to participate in persisting levels of inflammation and increased risk of non-AIDS comorbidities in ART-treated PLWH [ 2 , 4 – 6 ]. Gut damage and microbial translocation have been recurrently associated with inflammation and increased risk of non-AIDS comorbidities in ART-treated PLWH such as adiposity [ 7 ], cardiopulmonary function [ 3 ], and neurocognitive impairment [ 8 – 10 ]. LPS levels have been associated with HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND), especially in PLWH with hepatitis C infection [ 11 ], and with slower processing speed in suppressed alcohol heavy drinkers [ 12 ]. Circulating BDG levels have been associated with neurocognitive performance assessed with Global Deficit Score (GDS) [ 8 , 9 ]. Markers of gut damage, bacterial and fungal translocations have not been compared in their association with neurocognitive performance in ART-treated PLWH. We performed such comparisons in a well characterized group of ART-treated men living with HIV. Cognition was assessed in two ways: performance-based cognitive ability was quantified using the B-CAM [ 13 ]; and self-reported cognitive difficulties were documented with the 20-item Patient Deficit Questionnaire (PDQ) that assess memory (retrospective and prospective), attention, organization and planning over the previous 4 weeks.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the association between markers of gut damage, permeability, and microbial translocation (I-FABP, REG3α, LPS, BDG) and cognitive function (performance-based B-CAM and self-reported PDQ) in a cohort of 80 ART-treated men living with HIV. The findings indicate that bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation and higher regenerating islet-derived protein 3 α (REG3α) levels are significantly associated with increased self-reported cognitive difficulties, while fungal translocation (BDG) and intestinal fatty acid binding protein (I-FABP) did not show consistent or significant associations with cognitive outcomes. The study concluded that bacterial but not fungal translocation was associated with cognitive difficulties in ART-treated men living with HIV.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants were men living with HIV, receiving ART for an average of 12 years (range 6.6–17.8 years), with HIV viral load below or equal to 50 copies/mL. The study focused on biomarker associations within this ART-treated cohort and did not report specific ART dose, intensity, or duration details, nor were dose-response comparisons investigated.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels (median 39.0 vs. 54.6 pg/mL, p=0.01) were observed in participants with self-reported cognitive difficulties (PDQ scores higher than the median 26.25). This association with PDQ was independent of age and education in multivariable analyses. Splines analysis showed a strong link with worse self-reported cognition (PDQ) between 20 and 70 pg/mL, though an unexpected positive association with performance-based cognition (B-CAM) was also noted in this range. Daily plasma levels vary and systemic levels induce inflammation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Bacterial product and marker of bacterial microbial translocation; can cross the blood-brain barrier; induces systemic and brain inflammation by activating monocytes; participates in disorganization of neuronal networks.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Men living with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy, specifically in relation to self-reported and performance-based cognitive difficulties, and chronic stimulation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Strongly associated with increased self-reported cognitive difficulties (higher PDQ scores) in ART-treated men living with HIV, independent of age and education, indicating detrimental effects of bacterial microbial translocation on cognitive health, brain inflammation, and neuronal network disorganization. Also linked to increased risk of non-AIDS comorbidities and dementia in AIDS patients.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels (3.3 vs. 5.1 ng/mL, p=0.004) were observed in participants with self-reported cognitive difficulties (PDQ scores higher than the median 26.25). While an increase in plasma levels was associated with lower performance-based cognitive ability (B-CAM values), this was not statistically significant in adjusted models. Splines analysis showed a similar but weaker link with worse self-reported cognition (PDQ).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Antimicrobial peptide produced in the gut lumen; its presence in circulation reflects gut permeability/damage and lack of gut repair, associated with chronic inflammation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Men living with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy, specifically in relation to self-reported and performance-based cognitive difficulties, and chronic stimulation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Marker of gut damage/permeability, reflecting lack of gut repair and heightened chronic inflammation. Associated with lower self-reported cognitive abilities (higher PDQ scores) and potentially lower performance-based cognition in ART-treated men living with HIV, suggesting clinical importance for meaningful cognitive outcomes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No statistically significant differences in plasma levels (median 963-1088 pg/mL across B-CAM groups; 1038 vs. 931 pg/mL, p=0.97 between PDQ groups) were found. Not associated with either performance-based (B-CAM) or self-reported (PDQ) cognitive abilities in multivariable analyses. Plasma levels vary daily in ART-treated PLWH.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Released into circulation upon gut epithelium cell death, serving as a marker of gut integrity/damage and microbial translocation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Men living with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy, in relation to performance-based cognitive ability (B-CAM) and self-reported cognitive difficulties (PDQ).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Did not show an association with either performance-based or self-reported cognitive difficulties in ART-treated men living with HIV in this study, suggesting it may not be a reliable indicator of cognitive impact in this specific context.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma levels (e.g., 16.0 vs. 13.0 pg/mL, p=0.15 for PDQ groups) were not significantly different across groups of varying cognitive abilities (B-CAM or PDQ) in multivariable analyses. While higher plasma BDG levels showed a small, non-significant protective effect on self-reported cognition (lower PDQ score) with an effect size of 0.27, this association was not statistically significant. Systemic levels can induce inflammation and are associated with cognitive dysfunction.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Fungal product and marker of fungal microbial translocation; can cross the blood-brain barrier; induces systemic and brain inflammation; can be associated with stronger immune functions by trained immunity, and participates in disorganization of neuronal networks.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Men living with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy, in relation to performance-based cognitive ability (B-CAM), self-reported cognitive difficulties (PDQ), and chronic stimulation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Fungal translocation (measured by BDG) was largely not significantly associated with cognitive difficulties in this study. It showed a weak, non-significant protective effect on self-reported cognition in ART-treated men living with HIV; its link with cognition requires further replication in larger cohorts, despite general associations with brain inflammation in PLWH.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Different abundance linked with variations in brain functions. No precise quantitative change or specific direction (higher/lower) associated with cognitive decline reported.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Mucin-degrading bacteria; component of gut microbiota; implicated in gut homeostasis and the gut-brain axis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Gut dysbiosis in PLWH, linked with microbial translocation and disruption of gut homeostasis.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Linked with variations in brain functions; implicated in disruption of gut homeostasis, gut permeability, and inflammation, which are associated with decreased cognitive abilities.
